entries.title: Split-modulus via coprime factors, recombine by CRT / multiplicativity
entries.body: To show $m \mid k$ where $m=ab$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$, it suffices to show $a\mid k$ and $b\mid k$ separately — the two combine because coprime divisors of a common number multiply. Standard reduction for composite-modulus divisibility claims like $24=8\cdot3$; avoids working mod 24 directly.

entries.title: Difference-of-squares factorization for $p^2-1$-type claims
entries.body: Rewrite $p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)$ to turn a statement about one number's square into a statement about two consecutive even integers flanking $p$. This is the standard first move whenever a divisibility/congruence claim targets $n^2-1$ or $n^2-c^2$.

entries.title: Excluding small primes (here 2, 3) is exactly excluding the prime factors of the modulus
entries.body: In "for every prime $p>3$" type statements, the excluded small primes are typically exactly the prime factors of the modulus in the conclusion (here $24=2^3\cdot3$). Check this correspondence first: it usually tells you which coprimality facts ($p$ odd, $3\nmid p$) drive the whole proof, and confirms the bound ($p>3$) is tight, not arbitrary.

entries.title: Don't conflate the two coprime-factor arguments
entries.body: When splitting $24=8\times3$, the divisibility-by-8 argument uses parity/mod-4 case analysis on $p-1,p+1$, while divisibility-by-3 uses $p\bmod3$ case analysis — they are independent case splits on different moduli. A common slip is to try to get both from one case split (e.g. only casing on $p\bmod 4$ and hoping it also settles mod 3), which silently drops the mod-3 argument.

entries.title: $N\mid24$ iff every unit mod $N$ squares to 1 (exponent-2 characterization)
entries.body: Kaidi–Perlmutter (arXiv:2008.02190, Thm C.1): $\forall \ell$ coprime to $N$, $\ell^2\equiv1\pmod N \iff N\mid24$. Explains structurally why 24 (not some other number) is the sharp modulus for "square of any integer coprime to 6" claims — $(\mathbb{Z}/24\mathbb{Z})^\times\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3$ has exponent 2, and 24 is maximal with this property. Durable fact for this field, reusable whenever a "$n^2\equiv1\pmod N$ for all $n$ coprime to something" claim appears.

entries.title: $24 \mid p^2-1$ for every prime $p>3$ (this session's proved instance)
entries.body:
Proved via $p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)$: $p$ odd $\Rightarrow$ one of $p-1,p+1$ div. by 4 $\Rightarrow$ $8\mid(p-1)(p+1)$ (exhaustive case split on $p mod4\in\{1,3\}$); $3
mid p \Rightarrow$ one of $p-1,p+1$ div. by 3 (exhaustive case split on $p mod3\in\{1,2\}$); $\gcd(8,3)=1$ combines the two. Generalizes verbatim to any integer coprime to 6 (matches ProofWiki's "Square Modulo 24 of Odd Integer Not Divisible by 3"), since the proof only ever used $2
mid p$ and $3
mid p$, never primality itself — primality only entered via Phase 0's observation that the excluded cases ($p=2,3$) are exactly the prime factors of the modulus.
